chapter10-mission1.original: Explain read a settlement layout using lesson evidence.
chapter10-mission1.revised: Read a model settlement plan to describe how its streets, buildings, and open spaces connect.
chapter10-mission1.alignment: How the depicted spaces connect, not every residents actual daily route. A model layout does not establish every residents route or every towns form.

chapter10-mission1.original: Explain a house could combine materials using lesson evidence.
chapter10-mission1.revised: Describe how a house could combine stone or brick with wood, using a lesson example.
chapter10-mission1.alignment: Examples could combine masonry and wood; check the particular building. One house type does not describe every familys dwelling.

chapter10-mission1.original: Explain look for light and air using lesson evidence.
chapter10-mission1.revised: Explain how opening windows can let air into a house, using the lesson diagram.
chapter10-mission1.alignment: A ventilation function, not a measured temperature for every house. An airflow arrow does not measure temperature or every residents comfort.

chapter10-mission1.original: Explain work and home could share a building using lesson evidence.
chapter10-mission1.revised: Use the lesson example to explain how one building could have spaces for work and family life.
chapter10-mission1.alignment: It models a pattern that needs evidence for a particular house and period. A model or later display is not a complete record of earlier daily life.

chapter10-mission1.original: Explain buildings have histories too using lesson evidence.
chapter10-mission1.revised: Use dated records to describe how a building was built, changed, or repaired.
chapter10-mission1.alignment: Construction, alteration and repair dates for the particular features. A conservation report is not automatic proof of every earlier appearance.

chapter10-mission2.original: Explain learning was more than a school building using lesson evidence.
chapter10-mission2.revised: Describe learning in families and communities as well as in schools.
chapter10-mission2.alignment: Earlier community learning existed alongside later institutional changes. A building alone does not establish attendance or the teaching that occurred.

chapter10-mission2.original: Explain investigate a named teaching book using lesson evidence.
chapter10-mission2.revised: Use the Doctrina Christiana source card to identify its teaching purpose and what it cannot tell us about its readers.
chapter10-mission2.alignment: A particular printed material existed, not universal reading or acceptance. A printed book does not establish every persons reading, understanding or belief.

chapter10-mission2.original: Explain language helped communication using lesson evidence.
chapter10-mission2.revised: Explain how languages in a teaching text could help communication without showing what everyone understood.
chapter10-mission2.alignment: It shows languages in that material, not everyones language ability. One bilingual text does not prove everyones language ability or identical understanding.

chapter10-mission2.original: Explain a school policy was not every learners experience using lesson evidence.
chapter10-mission2.revised: Explain why a school rule does not show who actually attended or what they learned.
chapter10-mission2.alignment: Actual access, attendance, teaching and learning in particular places. Access, recorded attendance and demonstrated learning are different questions.

chapter10-mission2.original: Explain study religious life respectfully using lesson evidence.
chapter10-mission2.revised: Describe evidence about religious life respectfully, without assuming what everyone believed.
chapter10-mission2.alignment: Describe the event and seek appropriate evidence for wider claims. History activities assess evidence rather than a students own religion.

chapter10-mission3.original: Explain unequal power was not unequal worth using lesson evidence.
chapter10-mission3.revised: Explain how social categories could affect power and treatment without making anyone worth less than others.
chapter10-mission3.alignment: Explain how the label affected power or treatment without ranking human worth. Colonial categories do not determine any persons human worth.

chapter10-mission3.original: Explain an office and a person were different using lesson evidence.
chapter10-mission3.revised: Distinguish the duties of a local office from what a particular person actually did.
chapter10-mission3.alignment: Evidence of the persons actual actions in that setting. Check place, period and particular responsibilities before generalizing.

chapter10-mission3.original: Explain labels could shape treatment using lesson evidence.
chapter10-mission3.revised: Explain how social labels could affect treatment without showing a person's wealth or whole experience.
chapter10-mission3.alignment: Use evidence for income and distinguish it from the classification. A category alone does not establish wealth, occupation or every experience.

chapter10-mission3.original: Explain compare opportunities in everyday life using lesson evidence.
chapter10-mission3.revised: Compare how different conditions could affect people's chances to take part in everyday activities.
chapter10-mission3.alignment: An opportunity can be differently reachable under different conditions. Fictional learner cards do not establish every historical households experience.

chapter10-mission3.original: Explain a named case: a petition from bacolor using lesson evidence.
chapter10-mission3.revised: Use the Bacolor petition example to describe a social category, a local role, and a request without assuming its outcome.
chapter10-mission3.alignment: A named category, local role and petition need to be understood together. A petition, an investigation and a final outcome are distinct evidence questions.

chapter10-mission5.original: Explain change and continuity can happen together using lesson evidence.
chapter10-mission5.revised: Use a lesson example to explain how some practices could continue while others changed.
chapter10-mission5.alignment: Continuity in a skill can accompany a change in use. A named example is not every communitys history.

chapter10-mission5.original: Explain compare the same question across time using lesson evidence.
chapter10-mission5.revised: Compare the same feature in sources from different times, noting what each source can show.
chapter10-mission5.alignment: Whether they show the same building and feature in comparable ways. Not visible in a source does not always mean nonexistent.

chapter10-mission5.original: Explain a new rule was not every outcome using lesson evidence.
chapter10-mission5.revised: Explain why a new rule does not prove that everyone experienced the intended change.
chapter10-mission5.alignment: Actual implementation, access, attendance and learning. Access, attendance and learning are different questions.

chapter10-mission5.original: Explain people took part in change using lesson evidence.
chapter10-mission5.revised: Describe how people helped shape changes even when their choices were limited.
chapter10-mission5.alignment: People could act within limits without guaranteed success. Agency does not mean equal power, unlimited choice or automatic success.

chapter10-mission5.original: Explain heritage can continue and change using lesson evidence.
chapter10-mission5.revised: Use dated evidence to explain how heritage could be kept and changed over time.
chapter10-mission5.alignment: Keep its date and seek earlier evidence for claims about earlier forms. A later object alone does not establish every earlier detail.

chapter11-mission1.original: Explain a claim was not control everywhere using lesson evidence.
chapter11-mission1.revised: Distinguish a claim of Spanish control from evidence of control in a particular community.
chapter11-mission1.alignment: Evidence of authority actually carried out in particular communities. One map or expedition does not establish lasting control of every community.

chapter11-mission1.original: Explain autonomy meant local decisions using lesson evidence.
chapter11-mission1.revised: Explain autonomy as making local decisions, without assuming that everyone had equal power.
chapter11-mission1.alignment: Local decision-making could continue without unlimited freedom or equal power for everyone. Autonomy is not equal power for everyone or the absence of rules and contacts.

chapter11-mission1.original: Explain contact did not automatically mean conquest using lesson evidence.
chapter11-mission1.revised: Explain why contact or an agreement does not by itself prove conquest or lasting control.
chapter11-mission1.alignment: Authority and local practice beyond that post. Treaty wording and an authors account need dated evidence of actual practice.

chapter11-mission1.original: Explain autonomy did not mean an unchanging life using lesson evidence.
chapter11-mission1.revised: Describe how communities could change and keep outside connections while defending local decision-making.
chapter11-mission1.alignment: People could adapt and interact while defending local authority. Resistance does not prove isolation or unchanged practices across centuries.

chapter11-mission1.original: Explain compare claims with community evidence using lesson evidence.
chapter11-mission1.revised: Compare colonial claims with evidence about community life, considering each source's date and purpose.
chapter11-mission1.alignment: Compare their dates, purposes and evidence instead of treating one label as complete. No single source automatically speaks for every person or period.

chapter12-mission2.original: Explain put each case in its setting using lesson evidence.
chapter12-mission2.revised: Place each uprising in its own time and place without assuming the uprisings were planned together.
chapter12-mission2.alignment: Their sequence, not proof that they were one coordinated event. Chronological order alone does not prove coordination or causation.

chapter12-mission2.original: Explain tamblot: a named bohol case using lesson evidence.
chapter12-mission2.revised: Describe the religious concern linked to Tamblot's uprising in Bohol using the lesson evidence.
chapter12-mission2.alignment: A named Bohol uprising connected with a religious concern in 1621. Limited biographical records do not justify invented conversations or universal motives.

chapter12-mission2.original: Explain sumuroy: forced labor and abuses using lesson evidence.
chapter12-mission2.revised: Describe forced labor and abuses linked to Sumuroy's uprising without assuming everyone joined for the same reason.
chapter12-mission2.alignment: That every resident in each affected place joined with an identical motive. A wider affected area does not prove universal participation or identical local experience.

chapter12-mission2.original: Explain basi: monopoly and local livelihoods using lesson evidence.
chapter12-mission2.revised: Explain how the monopoly on basi was linked to concerns about local livelihoods, distinguishing the uprising from later pictures of it.
chapter12-mission2.alignment: Separate the event date from the later making of its depiction. A policy concern and later depiction do not reveal every participants motives.

chapter12-mission2.original: Explain compare similarities without erasing differences using lesson evidence.
chapter12-mission2.revised: Compare the uprisings' settings, concerns, and actions while recognizing their differences.
chapter12-mission2.alignment: Compare their distinct settings, concerns and recorded actions without assuming one program. Entries, markers and art accounts support different claims and have their own limits.

chapter12-mission3.original: Explain concerns could overlap using lesson evidence.
chapter12-mission3.revised: Explain how religious and political concerns could overlap in a movement.
chapter12-mission3.alignment: Investigate both with evidence rather than force one exclusive label. A revolt label does not reveal every persons belief or aim.

chapter12-mission3.original: Explain dagohoy: a concern and local organization using lesson evidence.
chapter12-mission3.revised: Describe the concern linked to Dagohoy's movement and how people organized, without assuming everyone had the same reason for joining.
chapter12-mission3.alignment: Explain both the reported concern and later organization within their evidence. A trigger and an institution do not explain every person or every year of the movement.

chapter12-mission3.original: Explain apolinario de la cruz and the cofradia using lesson evidence.
chapter12-mission3.revised: Use the lesson evidence to describe Apolinario de la Cruz and the concerns of the Cofradia without inventing members' words or motives.
chapter12-mission3.alignment: Identify its commemorated concerns while keeping member motives and exact words evidence-dependent. A later summary does not supply every members words, motive or full event chronology.

chapter12-mission3.original: Explain a movements dates were not a lifetime using lesson evidence.
chapter12-mission3.revised: Distinguish the dates of a movement from a leader's lifetime, leaving unknown personal dates uncertain.
chapter12-mission3.alignment: Label it as the movement span and keep uncertain personal dates unfilled. Duration alone does not prove identical conditions or participants throughout.

chapter12-mission3.original: Explain compare institutions and people respectfully using lesson evidence.
chapter12-mission3.revised: Compare the movements' institutions and people respectfully without assuming they had one shared plan.
chapter12-mission3.alignment: Compare their particular institutions, people and evidence without assuming one coordinated event. A shared theme does not prove coordination, identical aims or outcomes.

chapter14-mission2.original: Explain a place is not a participant list using lesson evidence.
chapter14-mission2.revised: Distinguish where an event happened from evidence of who took part.
chapter14-mission2.alignment: A place name helps locate an event. Joining requires evidence about people and actions. A resident, participant and affected person are not always the same role.

chapter14-mission2.original: Explain one island, different movements using lesson evidence.
chapter14-mission2.revised: Distinguish the Tamblot and Dagohoy movements in Bohol by their dates and recorded actions.
chapter14-mission2.alignment: The Bohol uprising is dated 1621. The Bohol movement is dated 1744-1829. A shared place does not make separate movements one event.

chapter14-mission2.original: Explain read a claim about wider reach using lesson evidence.
chapter14-mission2.revised: Explain how a movement could spread without proving that everyone in each place joined.
chapter14-mission2.alignment: The marker links Palapag and 1 June 1649. It names spread into areas of the Visayas, Mindanao and Luzon. Reported spread is not proof that every resident joined or every local action was identical.

chapter14-mission2.original: Explain a named contribution in ilocos using lesson evidence.
chapter14-mission2.revised: Describe Gabriela Silang's recorded contribution in Ilocos without treating one leader's story as everyone's experience.
chapter14-mission2.alignment: Gabriela continued the Ilocos uprising after Diego. The named contribution belongs to an Ilocos case. A leader account is not a complete record of regional participation.

chapter14-mission2.original: Explain build a community evidence portfolio using lesson evidence.
chapter14-mission2.revised: Organize community evidence by case, place, period, and recorded action without filling gaps with guesses.
chapter14-mission2.alignment: Keep case, place, period and recorded action together. Different sources can supply different kinds of participation evidence. Missing detail is not proof that a community was unimportant.

chapter14-mission3.original: Explain recognize a recorded contribution using lesson evidence.
chapter14-mission3.revised: Describe Gabriela Silang's recorded contribution without assuming it represents every woman's experience.
chapter14-mission3.alignment: Gabriela continued the Ilocos uprising after Diego. Include the recorded contribution instead of stopping with one leader. One womans recorded action does not establish every womans experience.

chapter14-mission3.original: Explain indigenous communities made decisions using lesson evidence.
chapter14-mission3.revised: Use the Ifugao example to describe community decisions and resistance without treating all Indigenous peoples as the same.
chapter14-mission3.alignment: The research concerns Ifugao history. It examines resistance and strategies strengthening local organization. One communitys history is not every Indigenous peoples identical experience.

chapter14-mission3.original: Explain contact was not the same as submission using lesson evidence.
chapter14-mission3.revised: Explain why contact or exchange does not by itself mean a community gave up local decision-making.
chapter14-mission3.alignment: Contact and resistance can occur in the same history. Ask who maintained decisions about local affairs. An exchange alone does not prove total submission or equal power within a community.

chapter14-mission3.original: Explain a cultural role needs its own evidence using lesson evidence.
chapter14-mission3.revised: Use evidence about Tamblot's role as a babaylan without assuming that everyone with that role had the same gender, beliefs, or actions.
chapter14-mission3.alignment: CulturEd identifies Tamblot as a babaylan in Bohol. The uprising is dated 1621. A cultural role label does not establish every holders gender, belief or action.

chapter14-mission3.original: Explain study history with communities using lesson evidence.
chapter14-mission3.revised: Explain how working with communities can help historians study their contributions and different experiences.
chapter14-mission3.alignment: Research can include active community collaboration. Compare sources with their context and limits. Recognize contributions without making everyone a single story.

chapter14-mission4.original: Explain working together does not mean being identical using lesson evidence.
chapter14-mission4.revised: Identify evidence of a shared aim or action without assuming that people who worked together were identical.
chapter14-mission4.alignment: Look for a particular aim or action held in common. People can cooperate while retaining different experiences. A similar complaint alone does not establish a recorded partnership.

chapter14-mission4.original: Explain spread and coordination are different using lesson evidence.
chapter14-mission4.revised: Distinguish a movement spreading to more places from evidence that people planned actions together.
chapter14-mission4.alignment: The marker reports spread beyond Palapag. A joint plan needs evidence of actions organized together. A brief spread summary does not supply every local plan.

chapter14-mission4.original: Explain belonging could have more than one layer using lesson evidence.
chapter14-mission4.revised: Explain how people could belong to different groups without assuming that local belonging was the same as a modern national identity.
chapter14-mission4.alignment: The study concerns a particular Pampanga setting. It describes recognition as members of town communities. Local recognition is not proof of identical rights or a modern national identity.

chapter14-mission4.original: Explain investigate differences without blame using lesson evidence.
chapter14-mission4.revised: Use evidence to explore disagreements and different choices without blaming people for not joining.
chapter14-mission4.alignment: Ask which aims or conditions differed. Use records of the particular disagreement and choices. Not joining does not by itself establish disloyalty or lack of courage.

chapter14-mission4.original: Explain trace a wider sense of belonging using lesson evidence.
chapter14-mission4.revised: Use dated words or actions to explain a wider sense of belonging, distinguishing it from a shared concern or joint action.
chapter14-mission4.alignment: Keep dates, groups and recorded words or actions together. Shared concern, joint action and identity are different claims. A wider sense of belonging needs evidence of that wider connection.

chapter9-mission1.original: Explain a required payment, not a gift using lesson evidence.
chapter9-mission1.revised: Explain tribute as a required colonial payment rather than a voluntary gift.
chapter9-mission1.alignment: A colonial obligation was recorded, not necessarily a voluntary gift. Recorded payment does not prove that a person approved of the demand.

chapter9-mission1.original: Explain payments could involve goods using lesson evidence.
chapter9-mission1.revised: Use a lesson example to describe payment in goods without assuming every community paid in the same way.
chapter9-mission1.alignment: Goods could be involved in that setting; other collections need their own evidence. A named item does not establish one amount or form for every community.

chapter9-mission1.original: Explain what did a payment mean for a household? using lesson evidence.
chapter9-mission1.revised: Compare how the same payment demand could affect households with different resources.
chapter9-mission1.alignment: The same demand can leave different resources available. Equal amounts demanded do not automatically mean equal burdens.

chapter9-mission1.original: Explain read the rule and the collection separately using lesson evidence.
chapter9-mission1.revised: Distinguish a tax rule from a record of collection, checking each source's date and what it shows.
chapter9-mission1.alignment: Compare their dates, coverage and recorded actions before explaining the difference. A complaint needs follow-up evidence to establish its outcome.

chapter9-mission1.original: Explain tax rules changed over time using lesson evidence.
chapter9-mission1.revised: Use the lesson timeline to describe the change from tribute to the later personal-tax system.
chapter9-mission1.alignment: One system ended while a later personal-tax system followed. A dated payment needs the rule that applied in its own setting.

chapter9-mission3.original: Explain crops had different uses using lesson evidence.
chapter9-mission3.revised: Explain how a harvest could provide food for a household and goods to sell.
chapter9-mission3.alignment: One crop can serve household and market needs. Sales received are not the same as income left after costs.

chapter9-mission3.original: Explain rules could change economic choices using lesson evidence.
chapter9-mission3.revised: Use the lesson models to explain how economic rules could change growers' choices about production or buyers.
chapter9-mission3.alignment: The growers choice of buyer. Check the product, place and period covered by the rule.

chapter9-mission3.original: Explain a named policy: the tobacco monopoly using lesson evidence.
chapter9-mission3.revised: Explain how the tobacco monopoly restricted production and sale in the districts it covered.
chapter9-mission3.alignment: Government control could restrict production and sale in designated districts. A monopoly period is not the whole history of a crop or every farms experience.

chapter9-mission3.original: Explain compare income, costs and choices using lesson evidence.
chapter9-mission3.revised: Use the fictional account to compare money received, costs, and money left over, and consider growers' choices.
chapter9-mission3.alignment: Three tokens in the fictional model. Check whether an account leaves out costs, work or payment delays.

chapter9-mission3.original: Explain follow a policy through time using lesson evidence.
chapter9-mission3.revised: Compare evidence before and after a policy ended without assuming all farming or trade stopped.
chapter9-mission3.alignment: A particular arrangement ended; later activity needs its own evidence. A reform date alone does not prove equal gains for everyone.

chapter9-mission4.original: Explain follow the pacific connection using lesson evidence.
chapter9-mission4.revised: Trace the Manila-Acapulco connection across the Pacific on the lesson diagram without treating it as an exact sailing route.
chapter9-mission4.alignment: A connection across the Pacific, not every exact sailing track. A schematic link is not the exact sailing track of every voyage.

chapter9-mission4.original: Explain goods and silver moved through a network using lesson evidence.
chapter9-mission4.revised: Describe how goods and silver moved through the trade network, distinguishing where goods were made from where they were loaded.
chapter9-mission4.alignment: Its loading port, not necessarily its place of manufacture. Examples do not establish every ships complete cargo or successful delivery.

chapter9-mission4.original: Explain look beyond the cargo using lesson evidence.
chapter9-mission4.revised: Identify work involved in making and moving cargo, including work that a merchant's record might not name.
chapter9-mission4.alignment: The account may leave workers unnamed; it does not prove they did no work. A merchant account may not name everyone who contributed.

chapter9-mission4.original: Explain a departure was not an arrival using lesson evidence.
chapter9-mission4.revised: Compare departure and arrival records for the same voyage without assuming that leaving meant arriving safely.
chapter9-mission4.alignment: The outcome of that same voyage. One outcome does not establish the result of every crossing.

chapter9-mission4.original: Explain connections did not mean equal benefits using lesson evidence.
chapter9-mission4.revised: Use evidence about people's receipts, costs, and choices to explain why trade connections did not mean equal benefits.
chapter9-mission4.alignment: Evidence about different peoples receipts, costs and choices. Ending this route did not end all Philippine trade.
